coreTruths.title: Bonding to tooth tissue is micromechanical infiltration, not chemistry
coreTruths.broaderContext: Adhesive dentistry sits underneath nearly every modern restoration. Resin tags into etched enamel and a resin-infiltrated hybrid layer in dentine are how everything sticks.
coreTruths.body:
## Etched enamel grips by porosity, not glue

Phosphoric acid opens up enamel into a porous, high-surface-energy surface, and resin tags flow up to 50µm in to lock the composite on [1]. 30 to 50 percent buffered phosphoric acid for 15 to 20 seconds is what produces that pattern, and 15 seconds on dentine [2]. Saliva contamination for as little as half a second wrecks it, so isolation matters more than any product choice [3].

## Dentine bonds through a resin-infiltrated hybrid layer

Dentine is wet, organic, and capped by a smear layer after cutting. The bond depends on demineralising the surface, keeping the exposed collagen propped up with moisture (not saliva), and infiltrating it with a bifunctional resin whose hydrophilic end grips wet collagen and whose hydrophobic end grips composite [4]. The molecular tangle in that hybrid layer is the bond. No technique has been shown to give zero microleakage [5].

## Etch and rinse for enamel, self-etch when only dentine is present

When enamel is in the margin, etch and rinse gives a stronger enamel etch [6]. When the margin is all dentine, like a crown prep, the milder acid of self-etch is gentler and tends to give less postoperative sensitivity [6]. Pre-curing the adhesive before placing the composite raises bond strength to dentine [7].

## Bonding to metal and ceramic uses the same logic

Metal surfaces get sandblasted for micromechanical grip then primed with a 4-META conditioner before luting [8]. Ceramics get etched (with hydrofluoric) then silanated [8]. Different surfaces, same idea: roughen, prime, lute.

citations.quote: Composite resin tags may penetrate up to 50µm into enamel to give micromechanical retention.
30–50% buffered phosphoric acid provides the best enamel etch pattern. An etching time of 15–20sec is adequate for both 1° and permanent enamel, and 15sec for dentine is recommended.
Success depends upon adequate moisture control, as contact with saliva for as little as 0.5sec will contaminate the etch pattern.

Most dentine adhesive systems aim to modify and partially remove the smear layer, by the application of an acidic primer. This demineralizes the underlying surface, exposing the collagen and opening up the dentinal tubules. It is important to keep this surface moist to prevent the collagen becoming flattened (not with saliva, though!). This layer is then infiltrated using a resin with bi-functional ends: one hydrophilic end, which is able to bond to wet dentine, and one hydrophobic end capable of bonding to the composite resin. In this infiltrated hybrid layer molecular entanglement of the collagen and resin occurs, providing the basis for the bonding system.
No technique produces zero microleakage.

If enamel is present, it is usually better to undertake etch and rinse whereas at the other extreme when dentine only is present, e.g. a crown preparation, then the weaker acid of the self-etching technique may be preferable. Self-etching possibly leads to less post-operative sensitivity.
Pre-curing the adhesive bonding agent before placing the composite ↑ bond strength to dentine.

Metal surfaces are usually sandblasted to provide roughness for micromechanical retention then prepared with a 4-META-derived conditioner before application of a composite luting cement. Ceramic surfaces are usually etched then silanated before luting.

coreTruths.title: Composite shrinks as it polymerises, and that shrinkage drives most of its clinical problems
coreTruths.broaderContext: Polymerisation shrinkage explains post-op pain, marginal leakage, cuspal flexure, and the rules around incremental placement. It is the single biggest reason composite is harder to place than amalgam.
coreTruths.body:
## Shrinkage stresses the bond, the tooth, and the pulp

Composite contracts 1 to 4 percent as it cures [1]. That shrinkage pulls on the bonded walls, and when the bond wins, the cusps deflect and the patient bites tender. When the bond loses, the margin opens and microleakage starts.

## The C-factor predicts how much trouble a cavity will cause

The configuration factor, the ratio of bonded to unbonded surfaces, drives how much of that shrinkage stress the restoration has to absorb [2]. A deep Class I has a high C-factor and very few free surfaces to relieve the stress, which is exactly the cavity where bond failure, cuspal flex, and post-op sensitivity happen.

## Cure incrementally, because depth of cure is limited

Light cure does not penetrate deeply. Anything over 2mm needs to go in incrementally [3], and the practical depth of cure is half the thickness of set material when tested on a block [4]. Position the tip as close to the tooth as possible, since air attenuates the beam [5]. Bulk-fill flowables push that depth out to 4mm and claim less shrinkage and cusp deflection [6].

## Cuspal flexure and post-op pain are the everyday consequences

When a dentine adhesive is in play, polymerisation shrinkage is more likely to deform the cusps and trigger post-op pain. Incremental placement and curing keeps that under control [7]. Flowables sound tempting as a liner, but they are mostly resin and shrink heavily, so they are not the answer in the floor of a deep proximal box; RMGIC sits there better [8].

citations.quote: Polymerization shrinkage of 1–4%.

The C-factor (configuration) is the ratio of bonded to unbonded surfaces in a cavity. The higher the C-factor, the more likely the risk of effects of polymerization shrinkage (bond failure, cuspal deflection, post-operative sensitivity).
Preparations >2mm depth should be cured incrementally.
The efficiency of the light source can be tested by curing a block of composite. Practical depth of cure is half the thickness of set material.
Air attenuates light beam, ∴ position as close to tooth as possible.

Flowable technology has led to further developments in the ability to bulk fill with the addition of several new materials such as SDR® flow+ from Dentsply with a 4mm depth of cure. In addition, the data from this material and similar suggests ↓ polymerization shrinkage and cusp deflection.

When a dentine adhesive is used, polymerization shrinkage of composite resin is more likely to result in cuspal deformation and post-operative pain. An incremental filling and curing technique will help to solve this problem.

Predominantly resin with a reduced percentage of filler particles, and consequently shrink considerably on curing. Some advocate using them as liners or in the bottom of proximal preparations, but the high shrinkage precludes this. RMGIC is preferable in proximal preparations, which are below the cemento-enamel junction (bonded-base approach); however, they have a place in the marginal repair of restorations and some advocate their use for facial cervical margin restorations.

coreTruths.title: Glass ionomer trades strength for chemical adhesion and fluoride release
coreTruths.broaderContext: GIC fills the niche where bonding matters more than load-bearing strength. Knowing why it bonds, leaks fluoride, and stays brittle explains every clinical decision around it.
coreTruths.body:
## GIC bonds chemically by ionic exchange with tooth tissue

Glass ionomer adheres to enamel and dentine through ionic displacement: calcium and phosphate in the tooth swap with polyacrylate ions, and the polyacid may also be absorbed onto collagen [1]. It also bonds to the oxide layer on stainless steel and tin [1]. That ionic bond is why it sticks without acid etching the way composite needs.

## Fluoride release plus reservoir uptake is its signature, but the clinical payoff is unproven

GIC keeps releasing fluoride throughout the lifetime of the restoration and recharges when the surrounding fluoride concentration rises, the so-called reservoir effect [2]. Whether that translates into actual caries reduction has not been shown to be clinically significant [2].

## It is brittle and load-shy: tensile strength is 40 percent of composite

GIC is brittle. Its tensile strength is only 40 percent of composite resin [3]. That keeps it out of load-bearing sites and confines it to non-stressed roles. Single-surface GI restorations only survive at <40 percent across 10 years [4].

## Where it actually shines: linings, cements, deciduous teeth, and the proximal floor of a sandwich

The usable applications are luting, lining, fissure sealing, deciduous-tooth restorations, and the proximal floor below the CEJ in a bonded-base sandwich technique [5]. Type I lutes crowns and bridges; Type II restores; Type III lines (defer amalgam 15 minutes, composite 4 minutes); Type IV is the light- or dual-cure variant [5]. RMGIC adds resin and gets command set, easier handling, and better aesthetics, and is the workhorse for moderate-depth amalgam linings and sandwich proximal boxes [6].

## Water balance during set is critical

GIC needs a dry field [7] but cannot dry out either: absorbing water dissolves it, dehydration crazes it, so it has to be sealed with a waterproof cover such as light-cured bonding resin during the early set [8].

citations.quote: To enamel and dentine by: (i) ionic displacement of calcium and phosphate with polyacrylate ions; (ii) possible absorption of polyalkenoic acid onto collagen. Some authors recommend pre-conditioning the dentine, e.g. with 10% polyalkenoic acid (GC Dentin Conditioner™) for 30sec. Whether this ↑ adhesion is controversial. GIC also bonds to the oxide layer on SS and tin.

Due to fluoride release throughout the lifetime of the restoration. GIs are also able to take up fluoride when the IO concentration is raised, the ‘reservoir effect’. However, the therapeutic benefit of fluoride release has yet to be proven to be clinically significant.
Brittle material. Tensile strength is only 40% of composite resin.
Single-surface glass ionomer restorations have a relatively poor survival of <40% across 10yrs.

Luting cements for crowns, bridges, and orthodontic bands. … Restorative cements. There are two subtypes: (i) aesthetic and (ii) reinforced. Can also be used as a fissure sealant, for the restoration of 1° teeth (…… Material selection for intracoronal restorations, p. 84) and for repairing defective restorations. … Fast-setting lining materials. Defer placement of amalgam for at least 15min and composite for 4min. In load-bearing situations or where lining is exposed to the oral environment (e.g. in sandwich technique), use of a type II reinforced cement or RMGIC is preferable. … Includes the light-cure and dual-cure GI

These allow ‘command’ setting and help overcome the moisture sensitivity and low early mechanical strength associated with conventional GI. The acid–base reaction of GI is supplemented by the addition of 75% resin (hydroxyethyl methacrylate Bis-GMA). The initial set of the material is due to the formation of a polymerization matrix, which is strengthened by the acid–base reaction. They are easier to handle than conventional GIs and may be polished immediately after light-curing.
A dry field is essential.

Water balance during setting is critical. Absorption of water results in dissolution, and dehydration leads to crazing, ∴ cement must be protected with waterproof material, e.g. light-cured bonding resin, which acts as a lubricant for finishing and can then be cured.

coreTruths.title: Impression accuracy depends on dimensional stability, not just detail
coreTruths.broaderContext: Crown and bridge fit is decided at the impression stage. Each impression material has a different dimensional behaviour, and matching that to the indication is what protects the lab work.
coreTruths.body:
## Match the material to how accurate the work needs to be

Elastomers are indicated when accuracy is paramount, like crown and bridge work and implants [1]. Alginate is cheap, fits a stock tray, and is fine for opposing arches and study models, but it is not accurate enough for crown and bridge work, must be kept damp, and has to be cast within 24 hours [2].

## Addition-cured silicone and polyether are the workhorses for fixed prosth

Addition-cured silicone is dimensionally very stable, so impressions can be posted or stored before casting [3]. Polyether uses a single mix and a stock tray and is routine for implants and multi-unit crown and bridge cases [4]. Polyether is stiff at set, which makes removal awkward over deep undercuts or mobile periodontally compromised teeth [4]. Polyether absorbs water, so it cannot be stored next to alginate [4].

## Condensation silicone and polysulfide have specific limitations

Condensation silicone is cheap but shrinks and should be cast immediately [5]. Polysulfide is messy with a long working time and only really earns its place in complete denture cases [6]. Reversible hydrocolloid is accurate but tears easily and is not infection-control friendly [7].

## Watch out for setting-reaction interactions

Powdered latex gloves can retard the setting of putty silicones [3], and alginate can retard the setting of gypsum and damage the model surface [2]. These small process details can sink an otherwise good impression.

## Disinfect, then cast on time

Impressions are rinsed and immersed in 1000ppm available chlorine sodium hypochlorite or a glutaraldehyde-free disinfectant for 10 minutes; current protocols do not seem to harm dimensional stability [8]. Intraoral scanners are accurate enough to fabricate inlays, onlays, crowns, fixed bridgework, copings, and frameworks, with the bonus that sections can be rescanned without taking a fresh impression [9].

citations.quote: Indicated when accuracy is paramount, e.g. crown and bridge work, and implants.

Setting is a double decomposition reaction between sodium alginate and calcium sulfate. Popular because it is cheap and can be used with a stock tray. However, it is not sufficiently accurate for crown and bridge work. Impressions must be kept damp and cast within 24h. Alginate can retard the setting of gypsum and affect the surface of the model.

This type of silicone is very stable, which means that impressions can be posted or stored prior to casting. A perforated tray or rim lock tray is advisable as the adhesives supplied are not very effective. Up to five viscosities are manufactured, allowing a range of impression techniques. NB: powdered latex gloves (now rarely used) can retard setting of putty materials.

(e.g. Impregum™) Popular because it uses a single mix and a stock tray. The set material is stiff, although newer products (e.g. Penta Soft™) have addressed this and removal can be stressful in cases with deep undercuts or advanced periodontitis. Absorbs water, ∴ do not store with alginate impressions. Can cause allergic reactions. Routinely used for implant cases and crown and bridge work, especially when there are multiple preps.
These materials are relatively cheap compared with other elastomers, but prone to some shrinkage and should be cast immediately. Addition-cured silicones are preferred.
Messy to handle, but useful when a long working time is required. Use with a special tray and, although stable, cast within 24h. Not recommended except in complete denture cases.
This is accurate, but liable to tear. Requires the purchase of a water bath and is not infection-control friendly.

Impressions should be rinsed to remove debris and then immersed in a solution of sodium hypochlorite (1000ppm available chlorine) or a glutaraldehyde-free proprietary disinfectant such as Perform® for 10min. In general, dimensional stability of impressions seems unaffected by current protocols.

Current scanners are sufficiently accurate in capturing details required to fabricate most restorations including inlays/onlays, crowns, fixed bridgework, fixed partical dentures, copings, and frameworks.

coreTruths.title: Ceramics trade strength for translucency, and crack propagation drives every failure
coreTruths.broaderContext: All-ceramic restorations are chosen for aesthetics. Knowing where their cracks start, and which core or substructure stops them, is what makes the choice between PFM, lithium disilicate, and zirconia rational.
coreTruths.body:
## Glassier ceramics look better and break sooner

Dental ceramics live on a spectrum from amorphous glass to fully crystalline. The glassier the ceramic, the better the translucence and aesthetics, but the lower the fracture resistance [1]. That trade-off explains the whole product range.

## Failure starts as a crack on the unglazed inner surface

Ceramic is brittle. The main failure mode is crack propagation, almost always starting from the unglazed inner surface [2]. Everything that strengthens a ceramic restoration is essentially about stopping that crack: bonding the inner surface to metal, or backing it with a stronger crystalline core [2].

## Metal ceramic gets its strength from the substructure

In PFM the metal supports the porcelain, the inner surface is bonded so cracks cannot propagate, and the outer surface ends up under tension that further blocks crack growth [3]. The aesthetic price is gingival staining and bulky cervical contours, but success rates are good (94 percent at 8 years) [4]. The bonding alloy needs a matched coefficient of thermal expansion (helped by adding leucite to the porcelain), a higher melting point than the porcelain, and indium to drive bonding to the metal oxide layer [5].

## All-ceramic options scale strength up by adding crystalline phases

Feldspathic porcelain is largely glass and best for veneers. Lithium disilicate (IPS e.max) sits in the middle, with higher flexural strength and good optics [6]. Glass-infiltrated alumina (VITA In-Ceram) and polycrystalline zirconia (Lava, Procera) sit at the strong end and are used as cores layered with veneering porcelain [7]. Zirconia must be milled oversized because it shrinks 30 to 40 percent on firing [7].

## Repair and bonding follow the same rule: rough up, silanate, lute

Porcelain repairs use composite plus a silane coupling agent [8]. For luting, ceramic surfaces are etched (hydrofluoric for feldspathic and lithium disilicate) then silanated before composite luting [9]. Composite-based luting is mandatory for ceramic and porcelain inlays, onlays, and veneers [10].

citations.quote: Dental ceramics exist in a spectrum from exclusively non-crystalline amorphous glasses through a combination of glass and crystalline mixtures to all-crystalline. In general, the ‘glassier’ the ceramic: ↑ translucence, ↑ aesthetics, but ↓ fracture resistance.

Brittle. The main cause of failure is crack propagation which almost invariably emanates from the unglazed inner surface. This can be ↓ by: Fusion of the inner surface to metal, as in the platinum foil and metal-bonded techniques. The use of a strengthened porcelain core.

The metal substructure supporting the porcelain. ↓ crack propagation by bonding the inner surface of the porcelain to metal. The outer surface of porcelain being under tension, thus ↓ crack propagation.
Good success rates reported (94% at 8yrs).

Higher melting point than porcelain. Similar coefficient of thermal expansion to porcelain (leucite used in the porcelain to bring it closer to that of the metal). Will not discolour the porcelain. High modulus of elasticity (rigidity) to avoid flexure and # of porcelain. Ability to bond to the porcelain to avoid detachment.

A specific popular variant has the usual aluminosilicate glass enhanced with lithium dioxide to give lithium disilicate glass in the form of IPS e.max®. The manufacturer claims ↑ flexural strength as well as ↑ optical properties via light transmission.

The final category is the polycrystalline form of dental ceramic. Unable to be pressed, the zirconium oxide used in this technique must be oversized initially to compensate for firing shrinkage. This is either done by machining an oversized framework for firing (e.g. 3M ESPE Lava™) or fabrication of an oversized die on which the framework is constructed for firing (Nobel Procera™).
Can be carried out using composite and a silane coupling agent. A number of proprietary kits (e.g. Cojet™) are available.
Ceramic surfaces are usually etched then silanated before luting.
Composite-based luting systems are often used in conjunction with dentine adhesive systems. Mandatory for cementing ceramic or porcelain inlays/onlays and ceramic veneers.

coreTruths.title: Amalgam's real risk is mercury vapour to the team, and it is being phased out for environmental reasons
coreTruths.broaderContext: Amalgam is still around because it handles well and lasts. The hazard profile is mostly occupational and environmental. Knowing this separates clinical reality from tabloid panic.
coreTruths.body:
## High-copper amalgams have outclassed the old conventional ones

High-copper amalgams (10 to 30 percent copper) react out the weak Sn-Hg gamma-2 phase. They cost more but are superior in corrosion resistance, creep, strength, and durability of marginal integrity [1]. Spheroidal particles give a more fluid mix, condense easily, can be carved immediately, and reach occlusal strength in 3 hours versus over 6 hours for lathe-cut [1]. Maximum strength still takes 24 hours, so patients should not chew on the tooth during that window [2].

## The actual mercury hazard is vapour, mostly to the dental team

The greatest actual risk from amalgam is inhalation of mercury vapour, and the dental team is theoretically at risk along with the patient [3]. Spillage prevention, encapsulated systems, mask and high-volume aspiration when removing old amalgam, and amalgam separators on suction lines are the practical controls [4].

## Allergy is rare; lichenoid reactions are the realistic clinical link

Genuine amalgam allergy is rarer than the press suggests; for proven cases composite or cast restorations are the alternative [5]. There is a documented link between allergy to amalgam constituents and lichenoid eruptions in the oral cavity in certain patients [6].

## The 2017 Mercury Regulations are environmental, not safety-driven

UK Control of Mercury Regulations 2017 ban amalgam in deciduous teeth, in children under 15, and in pregnant or breastfeeding women, except where the practitioner judges it medically necessary [7]. These regulations aim to reduce environmental mercury and are not a statement that amalgam is unsafe in the mouth [7]. Norway, Denmark, and Sweden have already banned it for environmental reasons, and further phasing down is likely [7].

## Marginal seal improves over time, and there are interim aids

Amalgam corrosion products eventually form a marginal seal, but in the interim microleakage can be reduced with a cavity varnish or a bonding agent that also bonds to set amalgam, or by sealing a ditched but caries-free amalgam with a fissure sealant [8].

citations.quote: Particle shape—can be lathe-cut (irregular), spheroidal, or a mixture of the two. Spheroidal particles give a more fluid mix which is easy to condense, can be carved immediately, and take 3h to reach occlusal strength (compared to >6h for lathe-cut amalgams). Spheroidal amalgams are preferable for pinned restorations. Particle composition—the first (conventional) alloys introduced had a low copper content (5%). The weakest (Sn–Hg or λ-2) phase of the set amalgam could be eliminated by ↑ the proportion of copper, so a variety of high copper (10–30%) amalgams have been introduced that react to eliminate it. These are more expensive, but superior in terms of corrosion resistance, creep, strength, and durability of marginal integrity.
NB: maximum strength takes 24h to develop, so it is advisable to recommend patients do not chew on the restored tooth for this time where possible.
The greatest actual risk appears to be related to the inhalation of Hg vapour and as such, the dental team as well as patients are theoretically at risk.

Avoid spilling Hg if non-encapsulated system employed. Waste amalgam should be stored appropriately to prevent mercury vapour release. When removing old amalgams, safety glasses, masks, and high-volume aspiration are a wise precaution. Amalgam separation devices should be in use as per Hazardous Waste Directive (91/689/EEC).
Amalgam—although genuine cases of amalgam allergy exist, these are rarer than the tabloid press would suggest. For proven cases, composite resin or cast restorations should be used.
In addition, there is a link between allergy to constituents of dental amalgam and lichenoid eruptions in the oral cavity in certain individuals.

In Norway, Denmark, and Sweden, dental amalgam is banned for environmental reasons. The Control of Mercury (Enforcement) Regulations 2017 stipulate there should be no use of amalgam in the treatment of deciduous teeth, in children under 15yrs or pregnant or breastfeeding women, except when strictly deemed necessary by the practitioner on the grounds of specific medical needs of the patient. It is likely further phasing down will occur (possibly to a full ban!). These regulations aim to reduce mercury in the environment and are not a reflection on any specific safety concerns about amalgam.

While amalgam corrosion products will form a marginal seal in time, microleakage can be ↓ by the use of either a conventional cavity varnish (e.g. Copalite®) or a bonding agent (e.g. Amalgambond® or Panavia-21™) in the interim. The latter (an anaerobic resin adhesive) also bonds to set amalgam.

coreTruths.title: Metals survive the mouth by passive oxide layers, which is why titanium and stainless steel work
coreTruths.broaderContext: A warm wet mouth is a corrosive environment. Whatever metal goes in has to either be noble or form a passive oxide film. This is the principle behind titanium implants, stainless steel instruments, and the chromium content of base alloys.
coreTruths.body:
## The mouth is a corrosive environment, so noble or passive metals win

A warm, moist mouth provides ideal conditions for corrosion. Casting alloys are built around a corrosion-resistant base, usually gold, with other elements added to tune the properties. With the possible exception of titanium, all of them can affect hypersensitive individuals [1].

## Titanium's biocompatibility comes from its surface oxide

Titanium has good biocompatibility and is the workhorse for implants and their superstructures, and a denture base option for patients allergic to other materials [2]. Heat treatment after manufacture optimises the grain structure (small alpha grain size, well-dispersed beta phase, small alpha-beta interfacial zone), which improves cyclic fatigue and resistance to crack propagation [2].

## Stainless steel relies on a chromium oxide passive layer

Steel is iron and carbon. Adding more than 12 percent chromium produces a passive surface oxide layer, which is what gives stainless steel its name [3]. The dental version is austenitic 18:8 (18 chromium, 8 nickel), used as orthodontic wires and partial denture clasps [3]. Drawing the wire work-hardens it; bending in clinic also work-hardens it in the plane of bending, so trying to correct a bend tends to fracture it rather than reshape it [3].

## Cobalt chromium is the rigidity workhorse for partial denture connectors

Cast cobalt chromium has high proof stress and modulus of elasticity, so thin castings stay strong, rigid, and lightweight [4]. Modulus of elasticity is twice that of type IV gold, which makes it a good denture base, although less ideal for clasps. Casting connector and clasps in one piece is what tips most partial dentures toward Co-Cr in practice [4].

## Nickel and beryllium are the sensitisers and toxins to watch for

Nickel chromium alloys can trigger contact eczema in sensitive patients (often with a history of jewellery allergy), and beryllium-containing nickel alloys are carcinogenic, with risk mostly confined to the lab during grinding [5]. Beryllium-free alloys are increasingly available [5]. Nickel alloys also cast less accurately than gold and bond more weakly to porcelain via their oxide [6].

citations.quote: A warm, moist mouth provides the ideal environment for corrosion. To overcome this problem, dental casting alloys comprise an essentially corrosion-resistant metal (usually gold), with the addition of other constituents to enhance its properties. However, with the possible exception of titanium, all have the potential to affect hypersensitive individuals.

Good biocompatibility; used for implants and their superstructure and in patients with allergies to other materials as a denture base material. In its use for implants, the titanium can be subjected to post-manufacture heat treatment to optimize the grain structure (small α grain size and well-dispersed β phase with a small α–β interfacial zone). This improves the properties with regard to cyclic fatigue and crack propagation.

Steel is an alloy of iron and carbon. The addition of chromium (>12%) produces a passive surface oxide layer which gives SS its name. The SS used in dentistry is also known as austenitic steel (because the crystals are arranged in a face-centred cubic structure) or 18:8 steel (due to the chromium and nickel content). … Wires are produced by drawing the SS through dies of ↓ diameter until the desired size is achieved. This work-hardens the wire, but heat treatments are carried out to give soft, hard, or extra-hard forms. Manipulation of SS wire also work-hardens the wire in the plane of bending, ∴ trying to correct a bend is more likely to result in #.

Cast cobalt chromium is the material of choice for partial denture connectors because of its high proof stress and modulus of elasticity: thin castings are strong, rigid, and lightweight. Although wrought gold alloys are more suitable for clasps, the advantage of being able to cast connector and clasps in one means that cobalt chromium is more commonly used

Beryllium, present in some nickel alloys, is known to be a carcinogen. Provided the alloy is not ground, any risks are confined to the production laboratory. Beryllium-free alloys are becoming ↑ available.

75% nickel, 20% chromium. Used in crowns and bridge work. In latter, ↑ rigidity compared to gold alloys is an advantage. However, castings are less accurate than gold, and nickel sensitivity can C/I its use.
